blocks.section: Cathode Rays and Glowing Phosphors: The Screen That Gave AI a Face

blocks.quote: The Wireless Century
blocks.section: The Wireless Century

blocks.quote: Radio: The Invisible Network
blocks.section: Radio: The Invisible Network

blocks.quote: Radio begins with a laboratory demonstration that electromagnetic action propagates with finite velocity. Hertz's *Electric Waves* collects the researches in which he generated rapid electric oscillations with sparks and Leyden jars and detected their propagation through space (\cite[Hertz, 1893]{hertz1893electricwaves}). Marconi's 1897 patent, "Transmitting electrical signals," turned the laboratory effect into a signalling system (\cite[Marconi, 1897]{marconi1897patent}). Radio then became the first network without wires: broadcast, radar, navigation and, eventually, mobile data. The air itself became a medium for machine-readable signals.
blocks.section: Radio: The Invisible Network

blocks.quote: Cellular and Wi-Fi: The Network Without Wires
blocks.section: Cellular and Wi-Fi: The Network Without Wires

blocks.quote: A radio network that serves many moving users needs a way to reuse spectrum. The cellular concept does exactly that: MacDonald's 1979 paper shows how a cellular system within a limited block of frequency spectrum can serve large-scale mobile telephony by frequency reuse and cell splitting, with hexagonal geometry and the AMPS system as the practical realisation (\cite[MacDonald, 1979]{macdonald1979cellular}). Local wireless networks followed a different path: the IEEE 802.11 standard of 1997 specified a wireless LAN medium-access control and physical layer, creating the technical basis for Wi-Fi (\cite[IEEE, 1997]{ieee80211_1997}). Together, cellular and Wi-Fi made network access ambient rather than a place you went to.
blocks.section: Cellular and Wi-Fi: The Network Without Wires

blocks.quote: The Smartphone: A Supercomputer in Every Pocket
blocks.section: The Smartphone: A Supercomputer in Every Pocket

blocks.quote: The smartphone is the point where radio, low-power computing, a camera and a touchscreen became one device. Apple's 2007 launch described the iPhone as three products in one, a mobile phone, a widescreen iPod and an Internet communications device, with a large multi-touch display, a two-megapixel camera, desktop-class email, web browsing, searching and maps (\cite[Apple, 2007]{apple2007iphone}). The processor lineage behind such devices descends from the low-power RISC idea: the Acorn RISC Machine was designed as a complete system architecture for optimal implementation on silicon, aimed at the low-cost personal-computer market (\cite[Furber and Wilson, 1987]{furber1987arm}). The cellular standards that carry the data are specified by 3GPP (\cite[3GPP, 2026]{threegpp_specs}). The result is a sensor platform in every pocket, generating the images, text, locations and behaviour that later become training data.
blocks.section: The Smartphone: A Supercomputer in Every Pocket

blocks.quote: Each of these discoveries was made for a goal unrelated to artificial intelligence. Remove any one and the edifice collapses; together they are the silent infrastructure on which every inference runs.
blocks.section: The Smartphone: A Supercomputer in Every Pocket

blocks.quote: The Physics of Computation
blocks.section: The Physics of Computation

blocks.quote: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: The entire digital age rests upon the **transistor**, a device whose invention required understanding a branch of physics that did not exist until the 20th century. The story begins, improbably, with sand.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: Silicon dioxide (common sand) is one of the most abundant compounds on Earth. But transforming it into a substrate for computation required:
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: 1. **Quantum Mechanics** (1920s–1930s): **Max Planck** introduced the quantum of energy in \citetitle{planck}. **Niels Bohr** proposed the quantized atom in \citetitle{bohr}. **Werner Heisenberg** formulated matrix mechanics in \citetitle{quanten}, and **Erwin Schrödinger** developed wave mechanics in \citetitle{schroedinger}. Together, they revealed that matter at the atomic scale behaves according to probabilistic wave functions, not classical Newtonian mechanics. This theory explained why certain materials (semiconductors) conduct electricity only under specific conditions, a phenomenon that classical physics could not account for.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: 2. **Band Theory of Solids** (1929–1931): **Felix Bloch** applied quantum mechanics to electrons in crystal lattices in \citetitle{bloch}. **Alan Herries Wilson** then used Bloch's framework to explain semiconductors specifically in \citetitle{wilsonsemiconductors}, describing how energy bands and “gaps” determine whether a material conducts, insulates, or semi-conducts. This theoretical framework made it possible to *predict* and *engineer* the electrical properties of materials like silicon and germanium.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: 3. **The Transistor** (1947): **John Bardeen** and **Walter Brattain** at Bell Labs built the first point-contact transistor in December 1947, a solid-state device that could amplify and switch electrical signals. They published \citetitle{semiconductor}. **William Shockley** followed with the superior junction transistor, described in \citetitle{shockley}. The transistor replaced the vacuum tube, which was bulky, hot, fragile, and power-hungry. Without the transistor, Moore's Law is inconceivable, and without Moore's Law, LLMs are computationally impossible.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{first_transistor}: a plastic wedge pressing two fine gold wires against a slab of germanium. This unassuming device replaced the vacuum tube and inaugurated the age of solid-state electronics.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: The path from a grain of beach sand to a chip containing billions of transistors passes through some of the most abstract physics ever conceived. A researcher debugging attention heads in a Transformer model is, at the deepest physical layer, relying on quantum tunneling effects in doped silicon crystals, a connection so remote that it borders on the absurd, yet it is absolute.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: The large language model is, at bottom, applied physics: inference is an electrical signal in doped silicon governed by quantum mechanics, and training consumes energy generated by electromagnetic induction. Physics also supplied the mathematics — the Boltzmann distribution behind Boltzmann machines, the Ising model behind early recurrent architectures, energy minimisation behind energy-based learning, and the free-energy principle as a proposed unifying account of biological and artificial intelligence.
blocks.section: Quantum Mechanics and the Transistor: From Beach Sand to Thinking Silicon

blocks.quote: The Chemistry of Computation
blocks.section: The Chemistry of Computation

blocks.quote: If physics provided the theoretical understanding of matter, chemistry provided the practical ability to *transform* it. Every component of an LLM's physical substrate, from the ultra-pure silicon wafers to the rare-earth magnets in hard drives, from the lithium-ion batteries in mobile devices to the specialized cooling fluids in data centers, is a product of chemical engineering. Chemistry gave AI its body.
blocks.section: The Chemistry of Computation

blocks.quote: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_merlin_enchanteur} (Public Domain): Merlin the Enchanter dictating his prophecies to his scribe, from a thirteenth-century French miniature of Robert de Boron's *Merlin en prose* — the magician whose art promised to command the world and could not, emblem of the failed magic from which chemistry was born. Source: \citeauthor{img_merlin_enchanteur}, \citeyear{img_merlin_enchanteur}, \citealternativetitle{img_merlin_enchanteur}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: Before chemistry could purify silicon, it had to exist — and it was born inside failed magic. *Chemistry* descends from *alchemy*: the Arabic *al-kīmiyā* Europe borrowed was a loan from Late Greek *khēmeía* (*Khemeu* in the third-century papyri), traced in turn to the Egyptian *khem*, the "black earth" of the Nile \cite[the etymology]{alchemy_wiki}. Alchemy was the art of transmuting base metals into gold, distilling an *elixir of life*, and perfecting matter through a staged *Great Work* (*opus magnum*). Its *goal* was impossible — no chemistry turns lead into gold, no powder grants immortality — yet the craft behind it, transforming one substance into another by fire, reaches back to the first metalsmiths, five thousand years ago, and ran in parallel across Roman Egypt, the Islamic world, medieval Europe, China, and India \cite[overview]{alchemy_wiki}. The impossible aim is what made the *instrument* possible: chasing it, the alchemists built the laboratory.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_jabir_alembic} (Public Domain): an alembic as \citeauthor{img_jabir_alembic} drew and described in the eighth century, one of the earliest recorded distillation apparatuses. Source: \citeauthor{img_jabir_alembic}, \citeyear{img_jabir_alembic}, \citealternativetitle{img_jabir_alembic}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: That shift — from a *ritual* to a *reproducible sequence of operations* yielding a *reproducible result* — is the method of science and of the semiconductor fab: a written procedure, followed step by step, reliably gives the same outcome.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_alchemist_studio} (Public Domain): an alchemist in his studio, as \citeauthor{img_alchemist_studio} painted him, the bench crowded with the furnaces, stills, and vessels that were his true instrument. Source: \citeauthor{img_alchemist_studio}, \citeyear{img_alchemist_studio}, \citealternativetitle{img_alchemist_studio}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: \marginfig{libavius_alembics.png}{The \citealternativetitle{img_libavius_alembics} (Public Domain): the alembics and distillation vessels as \citeauthor{img_libavius_alembics} drew them in *Alchymia* (\citeyear{img_libavius_alembics}), a catalogue of the laboratory glassware that chemistry would inherit.}
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: Every one of these vessels — the retort, the alembic, the slow **athanor** furnace \cite[on the athanor]{athanor} — is the direct ancestor of the modern laboratory's glassware, and of the sealed, temperature-controlled chambers in which silicon wafers are doped, etched, and grown.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_paracelsus_portrait} (Public Domain): \citeauthor{img_paracelsus_portrait} (Paracelsus, 1493–1541), who turned the alchemists' dream of a universal *elixir* into the systematic preparation of medicines, the founding move of pharmacology. Source: \citeauthor{img_paracelsus_portrait}, \citeyear{img_paracelsus_portrait}, \citealternativetitle{img_paracelsus_portrait}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: Alchemy's dream of a perfecting *elixir* became, in his hands, *pharmacology*: the deliberate, repeatable preparation of active substances. The quest for a "universal medicine" that alchemists chased for a millennium still runs in the background of every drug-discovery pipeline.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_flaming_heart} (Public Domain): the "flaming heart" from an alchemical and rosicrucian compendium of about \citeyear{img_flaming_heart}, an emblem of the *Great Work*, the long staged process whose goal was never achieved and whose method was. Source: \citeauthor{img_flaming_heart}, \citeyear{img_flaming_heart}, \citealternativetitle{img_flaming_heart}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Alchemy: The Displaced Root of Chemistry

blocks.quote: Silicon Purification: From Sand to Semiconductor
blocks.section: Silicon Purification: From Sand to Semiconductor

blocks.quote: The journey from common beach sand (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) to a functioning microprocessor requires chemical transformations of extraordinary precision. In an electric arc furnace at about 1900 °C, carbon strips the oxygen from quartz and leaves metallurgical-grade silicon that is only 98 to 99 percent pure. That is not enough for a transistor. The Siemens process converts the silicon to trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃), distils the compound to separate it from impurities, and reduces it again with hydrogen at about 1100 °C, leaving polycrystalline silicon of 99.9999999% purity (nine nines) (\cite[Yan, 2019]{yan2019siemens}). This “electronic grade” silicon is then grown into single crystals via the \citeauthor{czochralski1918} process \cite{czochralski1918}. Without these chemical purification methods, transistors cannot function: impurity concentrations of even a few parts per billion alter semiconductor behavior catastrophically. The entire digital age rests upon chemistry's ability to produce materials of unprecedented purity.
blocks.section: Silicon Purification: From Sand to Semiconductor

blocks.quote: Doping: The Chemistry of Controlled Impurity
blocks.section: Doping: The Chemistry of Controlled Impurity

blocks.quote: A pure silicon crystal is a poor conductor. What makes it useful is the deliberate introduction of specific impurities, a process called **doping**. Adding phosphorus atoms (Group V) creates n-type silicon with excess electrons; adding boron atoms (Group III) creates p-type silicon with electron “holes.” The p-n junction formed at their interface is the basis of every diode and transistor \cite{shockley}. This is fundamentally a chemical process: selecting specific elements from the periodic table and introducing them into a crystal lattice at precisely controlled concentrations (typically one dopant atom per million silicon atoms). Without the chemist's understanding of how atomic species interact within crystal structures, there is no transistor and no computation.
blocks.section: Doping: The Chemistry of Controlled Impurity

blocks.quote: Photolithography: Chemistry as Nanoscale Sculpture
blocks.section: Photolithography: Chemistry as Nanoscale Sculpture

blocks.quote: Modern chips contain billions of transistors, each smaller than a virus. They are manufactured through **photolithography**, a process that is essentially chemistry performed with light. A silicon wafer is coated with a light-sensitive chemical called a **photoresist**. Ultraviolet light is projected through a mask, causing chemical reactions that either harden or dissolve the exposed resist (depending on whether it is “positive” or “negative” resist). The unexposed (or exposed) resist is washed away with chemical solvents, revealing the silicon beneath for etching or ion implantation. This cycle is repeated dozens of times to build up the three-dimensional structure of a modern processor. Each step is a chemical reaction, polymerization, dissolution, oxidation, deposition, performed at nanometer precision.
blocks.section: Photolithography: Chemistry as Nanoscale Sculpture

blocks.quote: Electrochemistry and Energy Storage
blocks.section: Electrochemistry and Energy Storage

blocks.quote: The lithium-ion battery, which powers every laptop, smartphone, and increasingly the backup systems of data centers, is a product of electrochemistry. John B. Goodenough's identification of lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO₂) as a cathode material (1980) and Akira Yoshino's development of the first commercially viable lithium-ion cell (1985) enabled portable computing. Without electrochemistry, there are no mobile devices generating the user data that feeds LLM training corpora, and no uninterruptible power supplies protecting data centers from outages.
blocks.section: Electrochemistry and Energy Storage

blocks.quote: Rare Earth Chemistry and Permanent Magnets
blocks.section: Rare Earth Chemistry and Permanent Magnets

blocks.quote: The hard disk drives that store training datasets rely on **neodymium-iron-boron (Nd₂Fe₁₄B) permanent magnets** and **cobalt-platinum alloy** recording media, materials whose magnetic properties were characterized through decades of solid-state chemistry research. The voice coil actuators that position read/write heads with nanometer precision depend on rare-earth magnets whose synthesis requires specialized chemical extraction from ore (typically through solvent extraction and ion exchange chromatography).
blocks.section: Rare Earth Chemistry and Permanent Magnets

blocks.quote: Cooling Fluids and Thermal Management
blocks.section: Cooling Fluids and Thermal Management

blocks.quote: As GPU clusters push thermal limits, data centers increasingly turn to **liquid immersion cooling** using engineered dielectric fluids, synthetic fluorocarbon compounds (such as 3M's Fluorinert and Novec series) designed through organic chemistry to be thermally conductive, electrically insulating, chemically inert, and non-flammable. The development of these specialized coolants is pure applied chemistry, formulated specifically to remove heat from electronics without damaging them.
blocks.section: Cooling Fluids and Thermal Management

blocks.quote: Chemistry did not intend to create artificial intelligence. It intended to understand and transform matter. But in doing so, from purifying silicon to synthesizing photoresists to engineering cooling fluids, it provided every material prerequisite without which no language model could ever be physically instantiated.
blocks.section: Cooling Fluids and Thermal Management

blocks.quote: The Hardware of AI
blocks.section: The Hardware of AI

blocks.quote: Every weight update in a modern neural network is an electrical signal propagating through silicon, coordinated by a clock, stored in volatile memory, and communicated across copper traces on a printed circuit board. None of these components was invented for artificial intelligence. The CPU descends from wartime code-breaking. RAM evolved from radar. The GPU was forged by video games. Networking grew from military resilience planning. Storage was driven by census-taking. Yet together, they form the physical body in which neural networks are incarnated.
blocks.section: The Hardware of AI

blocks.quote: The Space Program That Nudged the State of the Art
blocks.section: The Space Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: Of all the displaced prerequisites, one is not a material or a device but a *demand*: a computer that could not crash, could not be switched off, and could not afford to be wrong. NASA never pushed the state of the art, as \citeauthor{tomayko1988spaceflight} puts it, but nudged it often enough to matter \cite{tomayko1988spaceflight}. Real-time scheduling, redundant voting sets, distributed flight computers and software-first design all migrated from orbit into the terrestrial stack; the dedicated section on spaceflight below follows those threads in detail.
blocks.section: The Space Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art
blocks.section: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: The poles gave AI three things it could not get anywhere else: the oldest data on Earth, the first reason to aim a giant computer at the whole sky, and a benchmark of cold the next computer had to beat.
blocks.section: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: \marginfig{vostok_ice_core.jpg}{Vostok Station, Antarctica, and the caves cut into the ice sheet to store drill cores at −55 °C year-round. [Photo: Todd Sowers, Lamont–Doherty / NOAA, public domain](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wostok-Station_core32.jpg)}
blocks.section: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: \marginfig{eniac_1946.jpg}{Two of the ENIAC's programmers, Jean "Betty" Jennings and Frances Bilas, setting up the machine in 1946 — the computer that, with Charney's team, produced the first numerical weather forecast. [Photo: U.S. Army, public domain](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Two_women_operating_ENIAC_%28full_resolution%29.jpg)}
blocks.section: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: \marginfig{qubit_cryostat.jpg}{The FMN Laboratory team (Bauman University, Moscow) assembling the cryogenic stage of a superconducting quantum computer, cooled to near absolute zero. [Photo: Sergey Kushlevich, CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Measuring_a_qubit_leaves_no_room_for_error.jpg)}
blocks.section: The Polar Program That Nudged the State of the Art

blocks.quote: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)
blocks.section: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)

blocks.quote: The CPU's modern history begins with relay-based processors like Zuse's Z3 (1941) and the vacuum-tube ENIAC (1946), which used thousands of tubes to achieve speeds thousands of times faster than relays \cite[see ENIAC description]{eniac1946}. The transistor (1947) made miniaturization possible (\cite[Bardeen et al., 1948]{semiconductor}), and the **integrated circuit**, independently conceived by **Jack Kilby** (1958) (\cite[Kilby, 1958]{kilbyic}) and **Robert Noyce** (1959) (\cite[Noyce, 1959]{noyceic}), placed multiple transistors on a single die.
blocks.section: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{eniac_image}: the U.S. Army's 1946 photograph of the ENIAC in operation at the Moore School. The machine spans an entire room and fills it wall-to-wall with cables, vacuum tubes and function-table panels.
blocks.section: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)

blocks.quote: The leap to the **microprocessor** arrived in 1971 with the \cite[Intel 4004]{intel4004}, containing 2,300 transistors at 740 kHz. The relentless growth described by \citealternativetitle{mooreslaw} drove counts from thousands to billions. Key architectural innovations included **pipelining** (IBM System/360, 1964), **out-of-order execution** \cite[first in the IBM System/360 Model 91]{tomasulo1967}, **superscalar architectures** (1990s), and **multi-core processors** (IBM POWER4, 2001), acknowledging that frequency scaling had hit thermal limits. For AI, the CPU served as the sole training platform until the mid-2000s, but its sequential MIMD architecture proved poorly suited to the massively parallel matrix operations of deep learning.
blocks.section: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)

blocks.quote: Random Access Memory (RAM)
blocks.section: Random Access Memory (RAM)

blocks.quote: The earliest electronic computers used **delay-line memory**, first implemented in the \cite[EDSAC]{edsac1949} (1949). An alternative approach, the **Williams tube** (1947), developed by \cite[Freddie Williams and Tom Kilburn]{williamstube} at the University of Manchester, stored bits as charged dots on the face of a cathode ray tube, making it the first form of truly random-access electronic memory. It was used in the Manchester Baby (1948), the world's first stored-program computer to run a program, and later in machines like the IBM 701. However, it was unreliable and required constant refreshing of the display. The breakthrough in reliability came with **magnetic-core memory**, developed by \cite[An Wang]{wangcore} (1949) and Jay Forrester at MIT, which dominated from the 1950s through the early 1970s.
blocks.section: Random Access Memory (RAM)

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{williams_tube}: a Williams-Kilburn cathode-ray tube with its associated read/write electronics. Each bit was stored as a tiny patch of charge on the phosphor screen, the first truly random-access electronic memory.
blocks.section: Random Access Memory (RAM)

blocks.quote: The modern era began when \cite[Robert Dennard]{dennard1968} at IBM invented **DRAM** (1966), storing each bit as a charge in a capacitor. The \cite[Intel 1103]{intel1103} (1970), holding 1 kilobit, rapidly displaced core memory. DRAM capacity has followed its own exponential trajectory: 1 Kb (1970), 1 Mb (1986), 1 Gb (early 2000s), to modern DDR5 modules offering 64 GB per DIMM at bandwidths exceeding 50 GB/s. For AI workloads, memory bandwidth is often the binding constraint: **High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)**, developed by \cite[AMD and SK Hynix]{hbm2013}, provides the necessary throughput for GPU-based training.
blocks.section: Random Access Memory (RAM)

blocks.quote: The Motherboard
blocks.section: The Motherboard

blocks.quote: The motherboard physically and electrically connects all components. The modern form traces to the **IBM PC** (1981), which established standardized expansion slots. The evolution of bus architectures, from ISA (1981) to PCI (1992) to \cite[PCI Express]{pciespec} (2003), reflects ever-increasing bandwidth demands. For AI training, motherboard design determines how many GPUs can communicate and at what speed; proprietary interconnects like \cite[NVLink]{nvlink} provide up to 900 GB/s between GPUs, far exceeding PCIe alone.
blocks.section: The Motherboard

blocks.quote: Networking
blocks.section: Networking

blocks.quote: The digital networking revolution began with **packet switching**, independently conceived by \cite[Paul Baran]{baran1964} (1964) and Donald Davies (1965). This was realized in \cite[ARPANET]{rfc1} (1969) and universalized through \cite[TCP/IP]{cerfkahn} (1974). Key milestones for AI include:
blocks.section: Networking

blocks.quote: Training a frontier LLM may involve thousands of GPUs synchronizing gradients every few hundred milliseconds. The collective communication patterns (all-reduce, ring-allreduce) are as much “hardware” as the chips themselves.
blocks.section: Networking

blocks.quote: Storage
blocks.section: Storage

blocks.quote: For large-scale training, data is stored in distributed file systems (Lustre, GPFS) or object storage (S3), striping petabytes across thousands of drives at aggregate bandwidths of hundreds of GB/s.
blocks.section: Storage

blocks.quote: The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)
blocks.section: The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)

blocks.quote: The first dedicated graphics chips (e.g., the \cite[IBM Professional Graphics Controller]{ibmpgc}, 1984) were fixed-function pipelines. Programmable shaders (NVIDIA GeForce 3, 2001) made GPUs flexible, and \cite[CUDA]{cuda} (2006) provided the software bridge. Key milestones for AI:
blocks.section: The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)

blocks.quote: Google's **TPUs**, custom ASICs for neural network workloads \cite[first deployed in 2015]{jouppi2017tpu}, offer an alternative architecture, and the competition between general-purpose GPUs and specialized accelerators continues to shape AI hardware.
blocks.section: The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)

blocks.quote: The Power Supply
blocks.section: The Power Supply

blocks.quote: Modern GPUs alone draw over 700 W; a full training node may consume 5–10 kW. The evolution from linear regulators to high-efficiency **switched-mode power supplies** (1960s–70s) made dense computing viable. The 80 PLUS certification program (2004) drove PSU efficiency above 90%, a seemingly mundane achievement that determines the economic viability of large-scale training.
blocks.section: The Power Supply

blocks.quote: The Clock
blocks.section: The Clock

blocks.quote: Every digital computer operates to the rhythm of a **crystal oscillator**. The quartz crystal oscillator, developed by \cite[Walter Cady]{cady1922} in 1921 for radio, was adopted for computing to ensure billions of transistors switch in lockstep. Modern CPUs tick at 3–6 GHz. Without this temporal coordination, the parallel operations within a CPU or GPU would dissolve into chaos.
blocks.section: The Clock

blocks.quote: Convergence
blocks.section: Convergence

blocks.quote: None of these components was invented for AI. Yet remove any single element and the entire edifice collapses. The history of AI hardware is the ultimate illustration of the “displaced prerequisite”: a convergence of solutions to unrelated problems that proved inseparable once they met.
blocks.section: Convergence

blocks.quote: The Fab: How Sand Becomes an Accelerator
blocks.section: The Fab: How Sand Becomes an Accelerator

blocks.quote: The previous sections treated the chip as a component. This section treats it as a manufactured object, because a modern accelerator is not designed in a vacuum: it is the output of an industrial system that turns purified sand into patterned silicon, and then packages that silicon with memory, power delivery and cooling. Remove the fab and the design is only a file.
blocks.section: The Fab: How Sand Becomes an Accelerator

blocks.quote: Why Silicon Won
blocks.section: Why Silicon Won

blocks.quote: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's continental crust after oxygen, making up roughly 28 percent of it by mass (\cite[Taylor, 1964]{taylor1964crust}). It reaches the factory as quartz and sand, both silicon dioxide. The element itself was first isolated as an amorphous powder by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1824, and Henri Sainte-Claire Deville obtained crystalline silicon in 1854 (\cite[Weeks, 1945]{weeks1945elements}). Abundance alone would not have made silicon the substrate of the digital age. Germanium, the material of the first point-contact transistor in 1947, has higher carrier mobility, and early transistors were made from it (\cite[Bardeen and Brattain, 1948]{semiconductor}). Silicon won on three properties that matter to a factory more than to a physicist.
blocks.section: Why Silicon Won

blocks.quote: First, silicon grows its own oxide. When silicon is heated in oxygen it forms silicon dioxide, a stable insulator that bonds to the surface and seals it. Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derrick at Bell Labs showed in 1955 that this oxide protects silicon during diffusion and can be patterned to mask dopants selectively, and they patented the process in 1957 (\cite[Frosch and Derrick, 1957]{frosch1957surface}; \cite[U.S. Patent 2,802,760]{froschderick1957patent}). The oxide is what makes passivation possible, and it is what photolithography etches.
blocks.section: Why Silicon Won

blocks.quote: Second, silicon has a wider band gap than germanium: about 1.12 eV against 0.66 eV. A wider gap means less leakage and operation at higher temperatures, which matters when billions of transistors share one package (\cite[Sze and Ng, 2007]{sze2007physics}). Third, silicon is cheap and its ore is everywhere. Germanium is far scarcer and is recovered mainly as a by-product of zinc refining (\cite[USGS, 2025]{usgs_germanium2025}).
blocks.section: Why Silicon Won

blocks.quote: The manufacturing answer to germanium arrived in 1954. Morris Tanenbaum at Bell Labs demonstrated the first working silicon transistor on 26 January 1954, and Gordon Teal and Willis Adcock at Texas Instruments announced a production silicon transistor in May of that year (\cite[Tanenbaum et al., 1955]{tanenbaum1955silicon}; \cite[Teal, 1976]{teal1976singlecrystals}). The decisive step came five years later, when Jean Hoerni at Fairchild combined the oxide with a metal interconnect in the planar process, filed in May 1959 (\cite[Hoerni, 1959]{hoerni1959planar}). That process made the integrated circuit manufacturable. Silicon did not win because it was the best semiconductor. It won because it was the one whose surface could be controlled.
blocks.section: Why Silicon Won

blocks.quote: From Sand to Single Crystal
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The first transformation is chemical. Quartz is reduced with carbon in an electric arc furnace at about 1900 °C, producing metallurgical-grade silicon that is 98 to 99 percent pure. That is far too dirty for a transistor. The Siemens process converts the silicon to trichlorosilane, distils it, and reduces it again with hydrogen at about 1100 °C, leaving polycrystalline silicon of electronic grade, often described as nine nines, or 99.9999999 percent pure (\cite[Yan, 2019]{yan2019siemens}).
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The second transformation is crystallographic. The purified polysilicon is melted in a quartz crucible, and a small seed crystal is dipped into the melt and pulled upward while rotating. The liquid freezes onto the seed in the same crystal orientation. Jan Czochralski invented the pulling method in 1916 while studying the crystallization of metals and published it in 1918 (\cite[Czochralski, 1918]{czochralski1918}). Gordon Teal and Ernest Buehler adapted it at Bell Labs in the early 1950s to grow the first high-quality germanium and silicon single crystals (\cite[Teal, 1976]{teal1976singlecrystals}). The result is a cylindrical ingot with the continuous lattice that a transistor needs.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_czochralski_1956} (Public Domain): a silicon crystal being pulled from the melt at Raytheon in 1956. The induction coil heats the crucible, and the technician measures the temperature with an optical pyrometer. Source: George E. Meyers, \citeyear{img_czochralski_1956}, \citealternativetitle{img_czochralski_1956}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: Zone refining is the second purification trick. In 1952, William Pfann at Bell Labs passed a narrow molten zone along a silicon rod. Impurities prefer the liquid, so they are swept to one end while the rest of the rod grows purer (\cite[Pfann, 1952]{pfann1952zonemelting}). Float-zone silicon made this way is the purest silicon available, and it is used where very high resistivity matters.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The ingot is then cut into wafers. Diamond wire saws slice it into discs, and lapping, etching and polishing remove the saw damage and leave a mirror surface. The industry's largest standard wafer is 300 mm across and less than a millimetre thick (\cite[Hahn, 2001]{hahn2001wafer300}). One wafer is patterned with the same die repeated across its surface, then diced into individual chips.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_ingot} (CC0): a monocrystalline silicon ingot and several silicon rods in the Museum of Mineralogy in Munich. The ingot is the output of the puller, before it is sawed into wafers. Source: ArticCynda, \citeyear{img_silicon_ingot}, \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_ingot}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_wafer_300mm} (CC BY-SA 3.0): a 300 mm silicon wafer, the industry's largest standard size. The mirror surface is the polished substrate on which every layer is printed. Source: Peellden, \citeyear{img_silicon_wafer_300mm}, \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_wafer_300mm}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_wafer_dicing} (CC BY-SA 4.0): a processed wafer on dicing tape, with individual dies already picked up. The wafer is the unit of production, the die the unit of sale. Source: Khpsoi, \citeyear{img_silicon_wafer_dicing}, \citealternativetitle{img_silicon_wafer_dicing}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: From Sand to Single Crystal

blocks.quote: Printing the Pattern
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: Photolithography is the step that turns a flat wafer into a circuit. The wafer is coated with a photoresist, a polymer that changes solubility when exposed to light. A mask, or reticle, carries the pattern for one layer. Light projects the pattern through the mask, the exposed resist is developed away, and the opening is used to etch the underlying film or to implant dopants. The resist is stripped and the cycle repeats for the next layer. A modern logic chip may go through this loop dozens of times, and every layer must be aligned to the one below it.
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_photolithography_process} (CC BY-SA 4.0): the heart of the cycle. Photoresist is applied to the substrate, exposed through a mask, and developed. A positive resist keeps the exposed areas soluble and removes them; a negative resist hardens where it is exposed. Source: May lam, \citeyear{img_photolithography_process}, \citealternativetitle{img_photolithography_process}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: The idea came from printing, not from electronics. Photoengraving had been used to make printing plates since the nineteenth century, and printed-circuit boards used photoresists in the 1940s and 1950s (\cite[Levinson, 2005]{levinson2005lithography}). The transfer to silicon happened at Bell Labs: Jules Andrus filed a patent on photolithographic fabrication of semiconductor devices in 1957 (\cite[Andrus, 1957]{andrus1957photolith}). At the Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratory, Jay Lathrop and James Nall used a photoresist to pattern germanium for miniaturized circuits, and their 1958 paper introduced the word "photolithography" to semiconductor manufacturing (\cite[Lathrop, 2013]{lathrop2013photolith}).
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: The machines evolved through a sequence of optical tricks. Early aligners pressed a mask against the whole wafer, or held it just above the surface. Projection aligners such as the Perkin-Elmer Micralign, introduced in 1973, imaged the mask onto the wafer without contact, which kept defects down and extended the life of the mask (\cite[Perkin-Elmer, 1973]{perkinelmer1973micralign}). Step-and-repeat reduction steppers, such as the GCA DSW 4800 in 1975, projected a reduced image of a single field and stepped it across the wafer, making it possible to print features smaller than the mask itself (\cite[GCA, 1975]{gca1975stepper}). Later step-and-scan systems moved the mask and the wafer together during exposure, which improved focus across the field (\cite[Levinson, 2005]{levinson2005lithography}).
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: The next jump was the light source. In 1982 Kanti Jain and co-workers at IBM demonstrated lithography with an excimer laser, a pulsed ultraviolet source far brighter than a mercury lamp (\cite[Jain et al., 1982]{jain1982excimer}). The industry settled on krypton fluoride at 248 nm and argon fluoride at 193 nm. These deep-ultraviolet wavelengths became the workhorse of chipmaking for the next three decades (\cite[Levinson, 2005]{levinson2005lithography}).
blocks.section: Printing the Pattern

blocks.quote: EUV: Light at 13.5 Nanometres
blocks.section: EUV: Light at 13.5 Nanometres

blocks.quote: The most difficult step is printing the pattern at the smallest dimensions. ASML describes extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as using light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm, the cutting edge of lithography and the highest resolution available, and states that it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV systems (\cite[ASML, 2026]{asml2025annualreport}). EUV simplifies manufacturing relative to multiple-patterning with deep-ultraviolet immersion: one exposure per critical layer instead of several, fewer masks and process steps, and better yield and scalability for advanced logic and memory (\cite[ASML, 2026]{asml2025annualreport}).
blocks.section: EUV: Light at 13.5 Nanometres

blocks.quote: At 13.5 nm every material absorbs, including air and glass, so the beam travels in vacuum and is shaped by multilayer mirrors rather than lenses (\cite[Joo, 2014]{joo2014vacuum}). The light itself comes from a tin plasma: a droplet of molten tin is hit by a laser, vaporised into a plasma, and its emission is collected and focused (\cite[Tomie, 2012]{tomie2012tin}). The underlying idea is older. Soft X-ray reduction lithography with multilayer mirrors was demonstrated in the late 1980s, with experiments on a synchrotron beamline and demagnified patterns below 0.5 micrometres (\cite[Kinoshita et al., 1989]{kinoshita1989euv}). The industrial machine took another two decades; the physics was already in place.
blocks.section: EUV: Light at 13.5 Nanometres

blocks.quote: The Foundry: Designing Without a Factory
blocks.section: The Foundry: Designing Without a Factory

blocks.quote: The pure-play foundry is a relatively recent institutional invention. TSMC was founded in 1987 as a joint venture and incorporated as a dedicated foundry: it manufactures semiconductors using its customers' proprietary integrated-circuit designs rather than selling chips under its own brand (\cite[TSMC, 2026]{tsmc2025annualreport}). That separation let companies design chips without owning a fabrication plant, while the foundry amortized the enormous fixed cost of the plant across many customers. TSMC's own filing describes fabs as "largely fixed cost assets" whose economics improve as utilization rises (\cite[TSMC, 2026]{tsmc2025annualreport}). The fabless model is therefore not a detail of business history: it is why a startup can specify an AI accelerator and have it manufactured at the leading edge.
blocks.section: The Foundry: Designing Without a Factory

blocks.quote: The Cleanroom and the Ultrapure Drop
blocks.section: The Cleanroom and the Ultrapure Drop

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_photolithography_cleanroom} (CC BY 2.0): the photolithography laboratory in the London Centre for Nanotechnology. A fab is a contamination-control problem before it is a computer. Source: UCL Mathematical & Physical Sciences, photo by O. Usher, \citeyear{img_photolithography_cleanroom}, \citealternativetitle{img_photolithography_cleanroom}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: The Cleanroom and the Ultrapure Drop

blocks.quote: A fab is a contamination-control problem before it is a computer. VLSI yields require control of particulate contamination during manufacture, and the ambient air of the production facility is one source; measuring ultrafine particles of 0.1 micrometres or less in real time requires instruments such as the differential mobility analyzer and the diffusion battery (\cite[Donovan et al., 1985]{donovan1985cleanroom}). Water is the other carrier: ultrafiltration removes particles, colloids and large macromolecules from ultrapure water, and leak detection in membrane modules is a prerequisite for defect-free manufacturing (\cite[Ruth and Berndt, 2016]{ruth2016ultrapure}). The cleanroom is not a metaphor for precision; it is the physical condition under which a wafer can be patterned at all.
blocks.section: The Cleanroom and the Ultrapure Drop

blocks.quote: Advanced Packaging: Where Memory Meets Logic
blocks.section: Advanced Packaging: Where Memory Meets Logic

blocks.quote: A modern accelerator is not one die but a stack. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die using through-silicon vias and die stacking, reaching more than 256 GB/s while reducing power, and its packaging must solve reliability, thermal dissipation, package size and high-throughput stacking (\cite[Jun et al., 2017]{jun2017hbm}). CoWoS-R uses an organic interposer to integrate heterogeneous and chiplet components, with low-RC interconnect, signal isolation and design scalability; integrated decoupling capacitors suppress power-domain noise and improve HBM3 signal integrity at high data rates (\cite[Jeng and Liu, 2022]{jeng2022cowos}). The logic die and the memory are only useful together, and the package is where their electrical and thermal limits meet.
blocks.section: Advanced Packaging: Where Memory Meets Logic

blocks.quote: The Grid and the Cloud: Powering and Renting Computation
blocks.section: The Grid and the Cloud: Powering and Renting Computation

blocks.quote: The Energy Stack: Coal, Oil and Fission
blocks.section: The Energy Stack: Coal, Oil and Fission

blocks.quote: The grid does not create energy; it converts and moves it. The first stage is mechanical. Faraday's 1831 induction experiment turned motion into current; Siemens's 1867 dynamo paper and Gramme's ring armature made that current steady and cheap; Parsons's 1884 compound steam turbine made it fast and compact. Edison's Pearl Street station (1882) showed that a central plant could light a district, and the Westinghouse–Tesla AC system, with transformers and high-voltage lines, made the grid regional. The generator at the end of the line has not changed in principle since Faraday; only the fuel and the scale have (\cite{faraday}; \cite{siemens1867dynamo}; \cite{parsons1911steamturbine}; \cite{electricpowerhistorywiki}).
blocks.section: The Energy Stack: Coal, Oil and Fission

blocks.quote: The Grid: Electricity as a Utility
blocks.section: The Grid: Electricity as a Utility

blocks.quote: The electric grid is a machine for moving power, not just generating it. Tesla's polyphase AC patents of the 1880s made long-distance distribution practical by supplying alternating current and a method of converting and distributing it (\cite[Tesla, 1887]{teslaelectricmotor}; \cite[Tesla, 1888]{teslacurrent}). A century later the grid has become a binding constraint on AI. The International Energy Agency's central projection has data-centre electricity consumption roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, about 3% of global electricity demand, while consumption from AI-focused data centres grew by 50% in 2025 (\cite[IEA, 2026]{iea2026energyai}). The same report describes grids being stretched by the wave of project applications for data centres (\cite[IEA, 2026]{iea2026energyai}). A training cluster is therefore not only a collection of GPUs; it is a customer with a power contract, a connection queue and a cooling load.
blocks.section: The Grid: Electricity as a Utility

blocks.quote: The Cloud: Computation as a Utility
blocks.section: The Cloud: Computation as a Utility

blocks.quote: The cloud turned computing into something that could be rented by the hour. Amazon S3, launched on 14 March 2006, offered an application programming interface for highly scalable, reliable, low-latency storage at very low cost (\cite[Amazon Web Services, 2006]{amazons3_2006}). Amazon EC2 entered limited beta on 25 August 2006: a virtual CPU equivalent to a 1.7 GHz Xeon, 1.75 GB of RAM, 160 GB of local disk and 250 Mb/s of network bandwidth, at ten cents per clock hour, built on the Xen virtual machine monitor and booting from Amazon Machine Images stored as S3 objects (\cite[Barr, 2006]{amazonec2_2006}). Kubernetes, open-sourced by Google in 2014, added a portable, extensible, open-source platform for managing containerized workloads, with scaling and failover handled by the platform rather than by hand (\cite[Kubernetes Authors, 2014]{kubernetes_overview}). The result is elastic compute: capacity that can be acquired for a training run and released when the run ends.
blocks.section: The Cloud: Computation as a Utility

blocks.quote: The Warehouse-Scale Computer
blocks.section: The Warehouse-Scale Computer

blocks.quote: At scale, the unit of design is no longer the server but the building. Barroso, Clidaras and Hoelzle describe the modern data center as one massive warehouse-scale computer: a warehouse full of machines whose hardware and software resources must work in concert to deliver Internet-service performance, with a design, operation and cost structure of its own (\cite[Barroso et al., 2013]{barroso2013datacenter}). The IEA notes that AI is pushing data-center power density to the limits of today's technologies (\cite[IEA, 2026]{iea2026energyai}). The cloud is therefore not weightless. It is a warehouse, a power contract and a thermal engineering problem, and the abstraction of "renting a GPU" rests on all three.
blocks.section: The Warehouse-Scale Computer
